definition: So foolish or unreasonable that it seems laughable.
example: The movie's plot grew so ludicrous that the audience laughed during the serious scenes.
nuance: Ludicrous stresses that something invites laughter, while absurd can simply mean illogical, with no humor involved.
prompt: A seller lists a rusty bicycle with a flat tire for sale online.
options: Asking nine hundred dollars for a bike with a flat tire struck buyers as ludicrous.
The price was so ludicrous that buyers agreed it was fair and paid it at once.
The ludicrous listing was easy to follow because its photos were sharp and well lit.
The seller felt ludicrous about parting with the bike his grandfather once rode.
reasons: A wildly excessive price for a damaged bike is laughably unreasonable.
Something laughably unreasonable would not be judged fair and accepted.
This confuses the word with lucid; clear presentation is not absurd.
Sadness over a family keepsake is sentimental, not laughably foolish.

practice.prompt: A student explains to a teacher why a history report is three weeks late.
options: The student said a ludicrous weekend job had paid well enough to cover new textbooks.
The report was ludicrous, so the teacher praised its careful research and gave it an A.
The story that a seagull flew off with the report was too ludicrous to believe.
The teacher found the excuse ludicrous, so she believed every word and granted an extension.
reasons: This mixes the word up with lucrative; a well-paying job is not absurd.
Careful work that earns praise is the opposite of something laughably foolish.
An excuse so far-fetched that it invites laughter fits the word exactly.
An excuse that seems laughably unreasonable would not be trusted completely.
